1:
The opening particle ties Babylon's fall to mercy on Jacob, and the tie is causal. Calvin allows the word might merely connect the verse to the last but prefers to make it assign a reason, so Babylon is destroyed because God will have mercy on a people he cannot reject; the consolation he draws is that the whole world is governed for the salvation of the elect. Henry reaches it from the symmetry of providence: the injuries must be revenged and the yoke broken, and one prediction serves as promise to the one side and threatening to the other, as the same providence had a bright face toward Israel and a dark one toward Egypt. Gill puts it plainly, mercy to the one bringing ruin on the others.

How far the prophecy reaches is the real dispute. Clarke argues that the two names are used with design, each taking in all twelve tribes, and that the circumstances described did not in any complete sense accompany the return, so the whole prophecy must look beyond that event. Ellicott makes the passage a critical hinge: the words imply a prevision of the return and therefore of the exile, and the whole section anticipates the argument of the later chapters, so the question of its authorship stands or falls on the same grounds. Calvin treats the return as a slight foretaste, all these statements being referable to Christ. Gill finds the first accomplishment in the edict that sent them home and a further one in the latter day; Wesley divides it the same way, literally at the return and more eminently in the gospel.

Whether the promise of ruling over their oppressors was ever kept is pressed hardest by Ellicott. He grants the decree of return answered the picture in a measure, but insists the words paint an ideal to which no historical reality has yet corresponded, since no later period has seen this people ruling a conquered race; any real fulfilment is of the kind the Latin poet meant when he wrote that captive Greece took her fierce conqueror captive, the triumph so far lying in the victory of the nation's leading ideas. He notes too that a later chapter admits the proselyte on terms of equality where this one has him in subjection. Calvin locates the fulfilment in the apostles, Jews who by the word subdued the very nations to whom their people had been tributaries.

The strangers who join them are variously identified. Gill takes them for neighbours in exile who had a kindness for the captives, especially proselytes, supplying necessaries for the journey. Ellicott traces successive fulfilments, first in the support of Persian kings and satraps, then in the proselytes of the apostolic age, then in the admission of the Gentiles. Calvin observes what followed the return, that so far from assisting them the neighbouring peoples leagued to distress them and would have driven them out of the world, so the thing described belongs to the kingdom of Christ.

The day of rest is filled in from three directions. Keil and Delitzsch separate the words, one being trouble that plagues, another restlessness that wears a man out with care, and note that the verb is the form commonly used for procuring rest. Ellicott supplies the history, since a monarch bent on towers and palaces who had carried off the skilled labour would vex his captives with fear and hard bondage, and cites an Assyrian king's boast of making prisoners carry burdens and lay brick. Clarke adds a textual note, that two manuscripts and the older versions supply a word restoring the phrase to the form almost always used on such occasions, one among many instances of a word lost out of the printed copies. Calvin reads the repetition as concession to weakness, since we believe with difficulty when our affairs contradict the promise.
4:
What kind of composition the song is takes the most room. Clarke makes the word the general name for Hebrew poetic style, covering the sententious, the figurative and the sublime together, so that a prophecy with hardly a figure in it and a long poem of quite another cast can both bear the name; the Greek, he notes, turns it into a lamentation, taking it for elegiac verse of the longer sort. Ellicott has the generic sense specialised into a derisive utterance in poetic speech, the prophet appearing once more as a psalmist, and calls the Greek rendering singular. Gill agrees it is a taunting speech full of ironies, and observes that the older versions make it a mournful song, though sung by the church over her enemy it is rather a triumphant one. Calvin takes the word for sayings weighty and worth observing, and finds the ruin so great that it passes into a proverb, the question form carrying astonishment and ridicule.

Which king is meant is answered two ways that barely conflict. Gill reads it not of the monarch under whom the empire stood at its height but of the one in whom it ended, and treats him as a type. Henry takes in the whole monarchy that sank with the last of them, and describes the poem as prepared not to adorn a hearse but to expose the memory and fix a lasting brand of infamy on it.

The golden city divides them more. Ellicott allows that if the English stands it matches the epithet a Greek dramatist gave Babylon, but the word occurs nowhere else, and recent critics, with the older versions, prefer the task-master or the place of torture, the Latin about tribute coming to much the same; the marginal exactress of gold looks like an attempt to combine two etymologies. Clarke takes it for the golden coin paid over as tribute. Wesley says the people used the word of themselves, and it is given in their own tongue. Henry accepts that and turns it, asking how men get wealth but by squeezing it out of others, and setting against it the one city truly golden. Calvin thinks it denotes rather the covetousness and insatiable greediness to which that nation was subject.

The instruments of the fall are handled briefly. Ellicott distinguishes the two symbols, the staff being what a man leans on and the sceptre what he wields to smite, and corrects the following verse into a relative clause with the sceptre for its subject, reading a stroke without ceasing and a trampling that is not stayed. Gill and Calvin agree the breaking was God's own act and no work of chance, Gill allowing that a human conqueror was used and Calvin adding that the ungodly stand bewildered before such works, not seeing the reason in them.

The rejoicing of the trees is read at various removes from the letter. Keil and Delitzsch call it a distinctive peculiarity of this prophet to bring the forest in as living and speaking, and note that the phrase for breaking forth into singing belongs to him alone. Ellicott identifies the tree with a pine growing on the Lebanon range above the evergreen oaks, whose timber served for houses and ships though it ranked below the cedar, and lets the literal and figurative senses melt into each other: Assyrian kings boasted of felling forests wherever they conquered, and the fir and cedar were also natural symbols of kingly rule. Gill offers the same choice, a figure or else princes comparable to such trees. Wesley keeps the trees themselves, felled for her pride and luxury and now suffered to stand. Calvin makes the personification an amplification, since men silenced under a tyrant break out when he falls, and even the dumb creatures are brought in to say what the living dared not.
9:
The world below receives him, and the voices differ on how far the picture goes. Ellicott fills it in most: the shades are giant-spectres of departed greatness; the verb is masculine where the noun is feminine, which personifies the place; the chief ones are literally the bell-wethers of a flock whose shepherd is death; and even there the kings keep their majesty and sit on thrones apart from the vulgar dead. Calvin keeps it a figure, speech given to the dead as gladness was given to the trees, and the whole ironical: kings are met at their coming with pomp, and this one shall be met and honoured too, with the honour he deserves. Wesley turns the thrones into the sarcasm, graves being their only thrones now, paved and covered with worms for gold.

Who speaks, and how long, is in dispute. Keil and Delitzsch limit the shades to the one question of astonishment and give the rest back to the singers, asking why they should receive a new comrade with scorn. Ellicott ends the vision at the same point, though the song resumed afterwards is coloured throughout by it. Gill keeps the dead speaking on. Calvin reads the question as bitter jeering, since tyrants are so blinded by greatness that they think themselves half-gods, and death alone acknowledges how small the dimensions of men's bodies are.

The bed of worms is the same reversal in every hand. Keil and Delitzsch make the maggots a bitter sarcasm replacing the costly Babylonian rugs that had been the corpse's bedding, and Calvin has the dead say jestingly that he has a bed worthy of him, worms for tapestry and a worm for coverlet.

Whether the fallen star is Satan is the sharpest question, and all four who raise it say no. Clarke is the most heated: the context speaks of a Babylonian king, and it would be strange if the Spirit called the arch-enemy of God the light-bringer; he doubts the rendering altogether, deriving the word from a root meaning to howl and preferring, with the Syriac, Howl, son of the morning. Ellicott gives the philology, the shining one, the planet Venus, symbol of a power bound up with star-worship, and calls the English word singularly unfortunate, since its later Latin use for the devil has hidden from most readers that a king is addressed; the Greek and English equivalents, he notes, went the other way and became a name of Christ. Gill allows an allusion at most, making the fall a type of antichrist's. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the astronomy, the name coming in other ancient languages too from the planet's brilliance, the title son of the dawn answering to a classical parentage.

The mount of the assembly divides them two and two. Clarke makes it the mount of the divine presence, so named not because the people gathered there but because God appointed it as his meeting-place, taking the stars of God for the Israelites. Wesley agrees and adds the geography, the north being exact since the temple hill lay northward of Zion strictly so called. Ellicott denies it flatly, reporting that most modern scholars hold that reading untenable, and puts in its place the heaven where the gods the king believed in sat in council, citing hymns that speak of feasts in the silver mountains. Keil and Delitzsch argue it negatively, that the hill was neither a northern point of the earth nor north of the city, and trace the mistake to a misunderstood psalm.

The reversal is caught by two. Ellicott finds indignant sarcasm in the repetition, since the king does reach the recesses he spoke of, but they are in the pit and not in heaven. Calvin sharpens it: in a wide sepulchre the honourable dead lie in the middle, and this one is thrust into a corner.
16:
Who is looking narrowly at him is not agreed. Ellicott holds the scene has shifted from the shadow-world to the field of battle, where men gaze at the conqueror's corpse as it lies dishonoured, bloody and unburied. Calvin allows the words might be referred to the living but keeps the whole discourse in the mouth of the dead, and explains the gazing, since men stretch the neck at anything strange, and the death of so great a king was a prodigy the eye could scarcely credit. Calvin adds a figure the others do not, that tyrants for all their cruelty are like clouds pouring a sudden shower as though to destroy everything, and scattered in a moment.

The cruelty charged is read closely. Ellicott prefers the margin, that he loosed not his prisoners to their homes, and shows the practice from kings who boast of carrying captive kings off in chains of iron and keeping them chained like dogs in the palace court, one held thirty-seven years. Calvin sets it against the alternative, since conquerors sometimes release prisoners to win hearts, while tyrants prefer to be feared, thinking terror the only way to reign; their end is wretched accordingly, for they have God for enemy and men for haters.

The denial of burial is the centre, and one voice makes it a question of reference. Calvin will not limit the prophecy to one king, because history does not show that the greatest of them was denied burial; the Jewish story that his son had him dug up he passes over as a fable, on the authority of a father otherwise credulous enough, and concludes that a whole dynasty is described. Gill relates that story as the Jews tell it. Wesley applies the words to the last of the line, whose people would have had neither opportunity nor heart to bury him honourably. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the contrast, every other king being laid out within his own palace while this one lay far from the sepulchre meant for him; Ellicott adds that such sepulchres, like the pyramid graves, were called an eternal home and were often almost literally the palace of the dead.

The figure for the cast-out body varies. Clarke takes it for the tree abominated, the wood on which a malefactor was hanged, and reports from a Jewish authority that such wood was buried with the body lest it keep an ill name, the stone that stoned a man and the sword that killed him being buried with him for the same reason. Ellicott sees a scion mildewed and blasted which men fling away as loathsome, and makes the raiment battlefield clothing gathered afterwards to be burnt, lying unburied being, as with the Homeric heroes, the shame of all shames. Wesley keeps a rotten twig the pruner throws aside, and explains the stones of the pit from the custom of heaping stones on bodies thrown in.

Why the want of a grave is a curse is answered only by Calvin, twice. Burial is not necessary to salvation, he grants, yet to be denied it is justly a disgrace; the value set on it among all nations came from the patriarchs, whose bodies God commanded to be buried in hope of the resurrection, so that where the carcases of beasts are cast out as fit only to rot, ours are laid in the earth to be kept against the last day. At the next verse he turns it into justice: the man who laid the earth desolate does not deserve that she receive him into her bosom, since she covers the dead as she supports the living. Ellicott closes from the monuments, quoting a Sidonian king's tomb-curse that joins the two halves of this sentence exactly: no couch among the shades, no grave, no son or seed in his stead.
21:
Who is commanded to prepare the slaughter has a common answer with different edges. Keil and Delitzsch allow the Medes if any particular persons were in mind at all, and read the negative particle as a wish, that no Babylonian kingdom should ever arise again; they add from an inscription that a later pretender took the great name and claimed a descent he did not have, and that the last shoot of the royal house was killed as a conspirator's child. Ellicott widens it to any minister of the divine vengeance, and pauses on the principle: in the judgment of God as history shows it, the stroke falls of necessity on the last members of a cruel dynasty, and in that sense the fathers' sins are visited on the children, while behind the veil each soul stands on its own responsibility and may win pardon for itself. Calvin makes them executioners held in readiness, Medes and Persians and others, since the city was not wholly destroyed when the Persians took it.

The clause about filling the world with cities has been much emended, and the emendations are declined. Ellicott lists the proposals, ruined heaps, terrible ones, enemies, conflicts, and says there seems no need for change, since the words describe the boast of monarchs who built cities to perpetuate their fame, the Assyrian and Babylonian kings recording their building and their destroying with equal exultation.

The heaping of words for descent is deliberate. Ellicott notes that the term rendered nephew keeps its true sense of grandson, that every word capable of expressing descent is gathered to express an utter extirpation, and that the Hebrew adds alliteration, as our own bag and baggage does. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point from two pairs of alliterative proverbial words meaning the whole without exception, comparing an Arabic phrase pairing flint with pebble. Calvin observes that God now says he will do himself what he had just commanded others to do, which shows both that the ruin of wicked men is his own work though he employs human agency, and how far prophecy carries, the prophets by it commanding nations.

What creature takes possession is uncertain, and everyone says so. Gill gives a water fowl that makes a horrible noise by putting its bill into mire, then lists the owl, the osprey, the tortoise, the beaver and the hedgehog as rival guesses, noting that the Arabic name for the last is close to the Hebrew word. Ellicott admits naturalists are not agreed, reports hedgehog and porcupine from the older versions and four more from scholars, and argues for a water bird on two grounds, that the word stands elsewhere beside the pelican and here beside pools, and that the hedgehog keeps to dry places and does not roost on ruined capitals. Calvin reasons from the same conjunction that an animal found near water is probable, and finds it suits the site, which lay moist though not marshy between two great rivers. Wesley agrees on a fowl delighting in solitary watery ground.

The sweeping away closes the burden. Clarke follows the Greek into another image, plunging the city in a miry gulf, and observes that the prophet writing to Chaldeans uses words peculiar to their own tongue for the divine judgments; a large body of manuscripts, he adds, reads the plural. Ellicott keeps the English and insists the force of the image be felt, since Babylon is swept away as men sweep foul rubbish from a house, and the world is cleaner for its destruction. Keil and Delitzsch supply the mechanism, the waters held off by artificial defences now let loose, so the river without its dam lays the region under water; Wesley says the same from the other end, that works kept up at charge and labour were neglected once the city fell.
24:
Why the oracle turns to Assyria here is explained four ways. Ellicott calls the passage a fragmentary prophecy, possibly misplaced, possibly added as proof that what was fulfilled on Assyria would be fulfilled on Babylon too, the two being so closely connected in the prophet's thought as to be almost identified. Henry supplies the pastoral reason: the fall of Babylon lay almost two hundred years off, and the hearers might ask what it was to them and what assurance they had of it, so the ruin of the enemies then at their door is given as a present comfort and a pledge for their posterity. Calvin puts the objection in their own mouths, of what avail it can be that Babylon is destroyed after Babylon has ruined them, and answers that a proof of favour is held out, either already given or shortly to be given.

Whether the Assyrian here means Babylon under another name is disputed. Gill offers the identification and then rejects it, since the king of Babylon did not fall in the land of Israel, and prefers a return to the earlier prophecy about the invader, while allowing that some read it as an event already past. Clarke takes the two peoples for one on the authority of two ancient geographers, and thinks the specifying of God's own mountains important, since it may point to the destruction near Jerusalem and have a farther view. Ellicott finds the fulfilment squarely in that destruction, the mountains being the hills round the city where the army lay encamped, called his because they were sacred to him. Calvin will not fix the date but conjectures that the slaughter had already happened, so the prophet argues from a known deliverance to a future one. Henry adds the moral, that those who wrongfully invade God's land find it is at their peril.

The oath itself is examined for what it concedes. Gill notes that the Greek gives only thus saith the Lord, since on a rabbinic principle his word is his oath, and takes the addition as made for his people's comfort. Calvin makes it a remedy for a particular weakness, since nothing is harder to believe than the sudden ruin of men we see flourishing, whose brightness dazzles us until we can scarcely credit God when he foretells their fall. He then presses the form of words, which breaks off and leaves the greater part unsaid, and finds the reticence deliberate, a check on our own freedom with oaths, which burst from us daringly and at random.

The closing verses widen the sentence. Ellicott takes the words as pointing to a universal history, since the fall of Assyria and Babylon does not stand alone but forms part of a scheme embracing all nations and all ages; he sharpens the last clause too, more emphatically his is the outstretched hand. Wesley keeps it nearer, to the vast empire now held by one power and shortly to pass to another. Gill states it flatly, that nothing comes to pass which God has not purposed and nothing he has purposed fails to come to pass.

Calvin uses the repetition to answer two objections at once. To the charge that the prophet, or rather the Spirit, uses too many words, he replies that those who think so are not well acquainted with themselves, since no confirmation suffices however frequent and solemn; the two things set before us, purpose and power, answer to the two causes of unbelief, that we doubt whether God has fixed the thing and whether he can accomplish it. To the objection that God has changed his purpose, as when he spared a repenting city, he answers that what was preached there was not the secret decree but a word meant to rouse them, so no such case touches the constancy of what he has declared.
28:
Two voices object to the chapter division first. Calvin says the fifteenth chapter ought to have begun here, a new subject opening, and that the divisions are not so much made as torn asunder. Gill agrees that some begin it here, and not improperly, since from this point the prophecies belong to another reign. On the date, Ellicott notes that it is fixed either by the prophet or by his compiler so that it might be seen the words were not written after the event, and thinks the burden an answer to searchings of heart natural in such a year.

Whose rod was broken divides them five ways. Clarke gives it to the king who had subdued the Philistines two reigns before, and makes the serpent's root his house, from which the son now coming would prove a far more terrible enemy. Wesley rejects that, since the king had been dead thirty-two years and any joy at his death was long past, and rejects the late king too, who was smitten rather than smiting; he settles on the royal race itself, whose sceptre might be called broken because it had passed to slothful princes. Keil and Delitzsch say the same more exactly, the phrase meaning the rod which smote thee rather than the rod of him that smote thee, the Davidic sceptre having been shattered by the war with Syria and Ephraim. Ellicott looks outside Judah and makes the rod the power of the Assyrian king, the Philistines exulting in his death or the other's. Calvin accepts the older king but will not stop there, one man standing for the whole body of the people.

The firstborn of the poor are agreed and differently phrased. Ellicott takes them for those who inherit a double portion, not of riches but of poverty, and identifies them with a Judah brought very low, for whom plenty is promised while Philistia is left to famine with no remnant to return. Calvin says they held first rank among the wretched, and adds the figure the others leave out, that the people are sheep, which we must resemble if we would have God for our keeper.

The smoke from the north is the real disagreement. Clarke makes it no smoke but a cloud of dust raised by the march of the Judean army on a country lying south-west, and quotes a Latin poet on fields smoking with dust. Ellicott gives it to the Assyrians and offers a choice, either the smoke of burnt cities or, likelier, the torch-signals used on night marches, which lets him correct the last clause into there is no straggler at the appointed places, the troops meeting at a rendezvous the fiery column marks. Calvin reads the smoke as standing for the fire that follows it, and notes that either the Assyrians or the Jews may be meant, both lying northward, preferring the Jews without arguing against the other. Wesley takes it for Chaldea and a grievous judgment, and reads the last clause as saying that not one of that army will desert his colours.

Who asks the closing question is the last dispute. Clarke offers two answers on the strength of a variant, ambassadors of the surrounding nations coming to congratulate a victory, or, if the singular of the text stands, envoys of the Philistines themselves suing for peace. Ellicott takes the verse to imply an inquiry received or expected, and suspects that the whole series of oracles which follows was delivered in answer to such inquiries, the prophet's fame having spread beyond Israel so that men of different nations came to consult him; the words are commonly referred instead, he notes, to the embassies of congratulation after the great deliverance. Henry closes on the answer rather than the question, that Zion was founded as a refuge for the poor who flee from wrath.
